terms.definition: Pulling information out of memory, for example by answering a question before checking the answer, instead of rereading it.

notes.text: Rereading feels productive but mostly builds familiarity. Recall builds memory.

terms.definition: Reviewing material at gradually longer intervals, timed so each review lands just before you would forget it.
The finding that study sessions spread out over time produce longer-lasting memory than the same total time crammed into one session.
How memory of new material fades over time when it is not reviewed: fast at first, then more slowly.

notes.text: Formula: R = e^(−t / S), where R is the chance of recall, t is time since learning and S is memory strength.

terms.definition: How resistant a memory is to fading. Each successful, effortful review makes it stronger.
Taking a practice test improves later recall more than spending the same time studying, even without feedback.
A challenge during learning, such as spacing or mixing topics, that slows progress in the moment but improves long-term retention.
Mixing different topics or problem types within one study session instead of practicing one type at a time.
Practicing one skill or problem type repeatedly before moving to the next. It feels smooth but tends to transfer less well than interleaving.
Explaining an idea in your own words and connecting it to what you already know, often by asking how and why.
Learning by teaching: explain a topic in plain language as if to a beginner, find the gaps where the explanation breaks down, then fill them.
Grouping separate pieces of information into larger meaningful units so they are easier to hold in mind.
The small, short-term mental workspace that holds information while you use it. It can only juggle a few items at once.
The amount of mental effort a task demands of working memory. Too much at once makes learning harder.
A memory aid, such as an acronym, rhyme or vivid image, that links new information to something easy to remember.
A card with a prompt on one side and the answer on the other, used for active recall.
A way to schedule flashcards using boxes: cards you answer correctly move to a box reviewed less often, and missed cards go back to the first box.
A diagram of ideas connected by labeled links, used to see how the parts of a topic relate.
A full-length test taken under exam-like conditions to rehearse timing and find weak areas.
The share of practice questions answered correctly.
Working in focused blocks, traditionally 25 minutes, each followed by a short break.
Studying a large amount of material in one intensive session shortly before a test. It can help the next day but fades quickly.
Thinking about your own thinking: judging what you know, what you don't, and which strategies work for you.
Feeling that you know material because it looks familiar, when you could not actually recall or apply it.
